text.p: Here are the highlights of stories in the Danish press on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

--Leading analysts no longer see the need for the government to intervene in the Danish economy, following the latest data showing falling inflation and stable foreign trade and current account surpluses. A former economic wiseman, leading banks and other experts see no danger signals for the economy or any sign of overheating.

--The latest European Commission half-year economic report warns Denmark about the potential danger to the economic upturn of rising public sector expenditure, especially social benefits including state-subsidised early retirement schemes.

--Danish chewing gum manufacturer Dandy is to cut staff due to falling sales caused by import restrictions in eastern European markets notably ex-Yugoslavia and Uzbekistan. Dandy is also to speed up plans to move production to Russia, its biggest export market, because of a change in VAT rules for imports. Dandy already has a packaging plant at Novogrod, south of St. Petersburg.

--Conservative leader Per Stig Moeller has expressed willingness to cooperate with the ruling Social Democrat-led coalition on Denmark's 1998 state budget as rumours of premature elections in Denmark fade away. The budget has to be passed in the autumn, elections are not normally due until September 1998.

--Danish shipping and energy group A.P. Moeller's turnover is among the biggest in the Nordic region at an official annual 77.4 billion crowns but thought in reality to be over 90 billion crowns, exceeded only by Norway's Statoil and Sweden's Volvo & Ericsson.
